A_target.statement:
In [[Definition:Martin-Löf Type Theory|dependent type theory]] with function extensionality, for every type $C$ there is a function $\mathbf 0 \to C$, and any two such functions are equal.
That is, the [[Definition:Empty Type|empty type]] is an [[Definition:Initial Object|initial object]].

B_source.statement:
For every type $C$ there is a function $C \to \mathbf 1$, namely $\lambda x. \star$, and by the $\eta$-rule for the [[Definition:Unit Type|unit type]] any two such functions are equal.
That is, $\mathbf 1$ is a [[Definition:Terminal Object|terminal object]].

object_map.reformulation: Reverse the arrows: the unit type has a single constructor and trivial elimination, while the empty type has no constructors and an eliminator into every type.

validity_conditions: Uniqueness of maps out of 0 needs function extensionality, since it is proved pointwise by the eliminator.
Logically, truth is always provable and falsity proves everything.
proof_plan: $\mathbf 1$ has one constructor $\star$, so maps into $\mathbf 1$ exist, and the $\eta$-rule makes them unique.

Dually, $\mathbf 0$ has no constructors, and its eliminator gives $\mathsf {ind}_{\mathbf 0} : \prod_{x : \mathbf 0} \map C x$ for every family $C$.
In particular there is a function $\mathbf 0 \to C$.
For $f, g : \mathbf 0 \to C$, the eliminator also gives $\prod_{x : \mathbf 0} \paren {\map f x = \map g x}$, so $f = g$ by function extensionality.

Hence $\mathbf 0$ is initial, dual to $\mathbf 1$ being terminal; under Curry-Howard this is ex falso quodlibet.
{{qed}}
